meta.title: What Were We to Do?
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer uses rhetorical questions that make the reader feel the problem.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured part_1 147w at FK 7.0, part_2 109w at FK 6.8, part_3 102w at FK 4.4. The load is rhetorical questions that make the reader feel the problem.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from Booker T. Washington, Up from Slavery (1901), under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: Washington, Booker T. Up from Slavery. 1901. Project Gutenberg eBook #2376, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2376, accessed 2026-11-11. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: Extracted a single passage; the authoring pass will split long sentences and simplify rare words; no facts added.
source.survey: A school for freed people has more students than rooms and no money to buy a campus.

session.difficulty_basis: rhetorical questions that make the reader feel the problem

authoring_exceptions: part_3 measures FK 4.4, just below the 4-5 window; the passage's short rhetorical questions carry the load, and splitting further would lose them.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: All these ideas and needs came at us at once, with a weight that seemed almost too much to bear. What were we to do? We had only the little old shack and the empty church that the good people of the town had kindly lent us for our teaching. The number of pupils was rising every day. The more we saw of them, and the more we went around the countryside, the more we saw that our work only partly did what the people really needed. These were the people we wanted to lift up by the pupils we should teach and send out to lead. The more we talked with the pupils, who came to us from many parts of the state, the more we found that many of them mostly wanted school so they would not have to work with their hands any longer.
passage.part_2: A story from Alabama shows this. A colored man was working in a cotton field on a hot July day. He suddenly stopped, looked toward the skies. Said: “O Lawd, de cotton am so grassy, de work am so hard, and the sun am so hot dat I b’lieve dis darky am called to preach.” About three months after the school opened, when we were most anxious about our work, an old abandoned plantation came up for sale. It was about a mile from the town of Tuskegee. The mansion house—or “big house,” as it was called—had been burned. The owners had lived there during slavery.
passage.part_3: We looked the place over carefully. It seemed just what we needed to make our work effective and permanent. But how were we to get it? The price was only five hundred dollars. But we had no money. We were strangers in town and had no credit. The owner agreed to let us occupy the place if we paid two hundred and fifty dollars down. The other two hundred and fifty dollars had to be paid within a year. Although five hundred dollars was cheap for the land, it was a large sum when one did not have any part of it.

items.prompt: In the opening, what two buildings did the school have for teaching? Name both places the passage gives.

tutor_only.confirm: The little old shack and the empty church lent by the town.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The third sentence of part_1 states that they had 'only the little old shack and the empty church that the good people of the town had kindly lent us for our teaching.'
tutor_only.tell: The passage names two places used for teaching. Find the sentence that lists both buildings.
help: Reread the third sentence of part_1.
That sentence lists the two places the school used for teaching.
tutor_only.core_idea: The school had only a small old shack and a borrowed empty church to teach in.
accept_ideas: the little old shack and the empty church
an old shack and a church the town lent them
the shack and the borrowed church
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They name the burned mansion house or the abandoned plantation.
if_they_say.ask: Which part of the passage did you use? Look again at part_1.

items.prompt: The school had only a shack and an empty church. The number of pupils rose every day. How do these two facts connect to show the school's problem?

tutor_only.confirm: The two facts show the school had too little room for a growing number of pupils.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence 'We had only the little old shack and the empty church...' and the sentence 'The number of pupils was rising every day' carry the answer.
tutor_only.tell: The shack and church gave the school little room. Pupils kept arriving, so the space problem grew.
help: The school had only a shack and an empty church.
The number of pupils was rising every day.
tutor_only.core_idea: The school's small space could not fit the growing number of pupils.
accept_ideas: The school did not have enough room for the growing number of pupils.
The small shack and church became a problem as more pupils came.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: The student says the two facts show the pupils were poor.
if_they_say.ask: Which sentence tells about the school's space?

items.prompt: What conclusion do the facts about the abandoned plantation support but not state?

tutor_only.confirm: The plantation could be a useful place for the school.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentences 'an old abandoned plantation came up for sale' and 'when we were most anxious about our work' support this conclusion.
tutor_only.tell: Use the sale timing and location. Say what it could mean for the school.
help: The plantation came up for sale near Tuskegee. Think about what that could offer the school.
The sale happened when the school was anxious. Say what that might mean.
tutor_only.core_idea: The abandoned plantation may offer the school a place to use or grow.
accept_ideas: The plantation could give the school a place to grow.
The sale might solve the school's need for space.
The abandoned land could be useful for the school.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the passage states the plantation was bought.
if_they_say.ask: What does the passage say happened after it came up for sale?

items.prompt: The writer asks, 'What were we to do?' What does this question make you feel about the school's problem?

tutor_only.confirm: The question makes the school's problem feel urgent and pulls the reader into the leaders' worry.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The question comes right after the needs crowd in; it asks the reader to feel how hard the leaders' problem was.
tutor_only.tell: The writer asks what they could do instead of telling. The question makes the reader feel the leaders' worry and the problem's weight.
help: Look at what the man does right before he says he is called to preach. Think about why the author makes his call come suddenly during hard work.
tutor_only.core_idea: The rhetorical question pulls the reader into the leaders' worry and makes the school's problem feel urgent.
accept_ideas: The question makes the problem feel urgent.
It makes the reader share the leaders' worry.
It shows how hard the problem was.
It pulls the reader into the leaders' situation.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the question asks for a factual answer or a list of steps.
if_they_say.ask: What does the question make you feel about the problem, not what answer does it expect?

items.prompt: How does the writer's plan for the school's needs change from the opening to the last part?

tutor_only.confirm: The writer moves from a broad space and teaching need to one property and how to pay for it.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Part_1 carries the broad need: the pupils were rising and the work only partly met what people needed. Part_3 carries the shift to a concrete plan and obstacle: the abandoned plantation seemed what they needed, but the price was five hundred dollars, they had no money, and the owner required two hundred and fifty dollars down and the rest within a year.
tutor_only.tell: Part_1 shows a broad, urgent need for more space and better teaching. Part_3 narrows to one plantation and the problem of paying for it.
help: The need in part_1 is broad and urgent.
Part_3 names a place, a price, and a payment problem.
tutor_only.core_idea: The passage shifts from describing a general, urgent need to focusing on a specific solution and its practical funding obstacle.
accept_ideas: The writer moves from a broad, urgent need for space to a specific property and a payment problem.
Part_1 describes many growing needs; part_3 focuses on one plantation and the cost.
The plan becomes more concrete: buy the old plantation, but finding $250 down and $250 within a year is hard.
not_required: Every detail about the pupils or the Alabama story
The exact wording of the rhetorical question
A full retelling of the passage
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They retell the $500 price without naming the change in focus.
if_they_say.ask: What broad need from part_1 becomes a specific property and money problem in part_3?
